extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history/philosophy of mathematics and mathematicians interested in Bourbaki's methods
extracted.subtask_description: Examine Bourbaki's conception of mathematics (theory of structures, axiomatic method, selection of topics, formalization and style) and the implicit criteria they used for what counts as significant mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of mathematics via the axiomatic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is kept as an 'indivisible whole' by virtue of unified methodology and the discovery of analogies; the axiomatic method explains deep-lying reasons for 'unexpected support' between distinct theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert and Dieudonné: the axiomatic method provides a central nucleus and explains analogies between disparate branches; evaluation asks whether a development or presentation reveals such unifying logical devices and analogies (cf. 'The Architecture of Mathematics').

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of structures as a unifying tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of structures (the 'great types of structures') plays a central role in unifying large domains of mathematics and provides powerful tools that 'sweep over immense domains.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dieudonné: each structure 'carries with it its own language' that orients intuition and illuminates mathematical landscapes. Assessment focuses on whether identification of structures reveals unifying patterns and yields new directions for research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for inclusion in the treatise
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria used by Bourbaki to select topics initially emphasized external applicability/usefulness (e.g., for physicists and engineers), later shifting toward more abstract inclinations and perceived mathematical interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early criterion: external applicability. Later: subjective judgments of 'interest' informed by the group's intuitions and background; Dieudonné and Cartan note that selection is crucial and often based on deep familiarity and intuition rather than general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-of-interest / 'axiomatic trash' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all axiomatic systems are equally worthwhile: only a limited number of systems constitute active research disciplines; some systems are dismissed as 'axiomatic trash.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartan and others argued that theories 'built upon different axiomatic systems have varying degrees of interest.' Evaluation requires judging the research vitality and perceived mathematical significance of an axiomatic system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations of reflexive/formal justification
rubrics_metrics.description: There was an expectation that a reflexive (formal) mathematical theory could justify selection/choice of disciplines, but Bourbaki's theory of structures did not effectively provide such answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a formal theory was sought to classify fundamental disciplines, in practice choices relied on mathematicians' intuitions; therefore one should not expect purely formal proofs to settle the selection question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation style: systematic, rigorous, standardized notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki aimed at presenting mathematical knowledge in a systematic and unified fashion, within a standard system of notation and with uncompromising rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise emphasizes standard notation and axiomatic exposition; assessment of expositions should check for systematic organization, consistent notation, and rigorous axiom-based presentation—though some volumes show more heuristic material than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical partial formalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Full formalization is impracticable; treatise uses partial formalization with symbolic abbreviations and condensed deductive criteria so proofs need not display every inference step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book I presents a formalized language intended to permit formulation of all axiomatic systems but concedes to practical partial formalization. Evaluation of foundational material should accept condensed formal devices and symbolic shorthand as legitimate compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical stance on consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency of set theory (and mathematics) is treated empirically: a contradiction is not expected because none has appeared in long practice; consistency is considered an empirical fact rather than demonstrated by formal means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki avoids formal consistency proofs and treats absence of contradiction as historically grounded. When assessing foundational claims, note this empiricist justification rather than a proof-based guarantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-dependence of theoremhood and contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The status of a relation as a theorem or the notion that a theory is contradictory is dependent on the stage of development of the theory; theoremhood is relative to what has been inserted into proofs at a given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki explicitly notes that meta-mathematical concepts (theorem, contradictory theory) are time-dependent. Evaluations should therefore be contextual and sensitive to the evolving state of a theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of intuition and deep background in selection
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no general rule' to judge what is interesting in mathematics; selection requires thorough understanding, critical evaluation, or sudden intuition—decisions often rest on individual mathematicians' expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartan: only deep familiarity with many theories and informed intuition justify choices. Assessments of mathematical importance must therefore account for expert judgment and tacit knowledge—not merely formal criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensions between standardization and creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki's program exposed dualities: standardized techniques vs. ingenuity in problem-solving; collective work vs. individual genius; formalized generalization vs. intuitive grasp of specific situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should be alert to these tensions: a work might be strong in formal/systematic presentation but still lack the intuitive insights or problem-solving originality prized by practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and organization of foundational volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatise organizes 'Fundamental Structures of Analysis' into core books (Sets, Algebra, General Topology, Functions of a Real Variable, etc.), with the theory of structures placed in Book I (Set Theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a comprehensive foundational project, check the chosen organizational scheme (which topics are core vs. supplementary) and whether the placement of foundational material (e.g., set theory) supports the claimed unifying role.
